quiz.question: What is the main purpose of system hardening?
options: Disable as many operating system features as possible
Reduce unnecessary exposure while preserving required functionality
Grant all users administrative permissions
Replace patching with firewall rules
quiz.explanation: System hardening is the deliberate process of reducing unnecessary system capabilities, interfaces, services, and attack surfaces while aligning security settings with the system's required operational role. Blindly disabling features without considering functionality is poor engineering.

quiz.question: On a typical Linux system, what does mode 640 mean?
options: Everyone can read and write
Owner and group have full access
Owner can read/write, group can read, other users have no access through these mode bits
Only the group can execute the file
quiz.explanation: In octal notation, 6 = Read (4) + Write (2); 4 = Read (4); 0 = No permissions (0). Thus, mode 640 grants read/write to the owner, read-only to the group, and zero access to other users.

quiz.question: Why is least privilege important for service accounts?
options: It limits the damage a compromised service can cause
It ensures every service runs as root
It removes the need for audit logs
It allows services to bypass file permissions
quiz.explanation: If a service account runs with minimal permissions (e.g. read-only on static files, no shell access, no sudo), an attacker who compromises the application cannot easily tamper with OS binaries, pivot laterally, or escalate to root.

quiz.question: What is an important role of Windows UAC?
options: Automatically encrypt every file
Support standard-user operation and controlled elevation for privileged tasks
Replace NTFS permissions
Guarantee that all applications are safe
quiz.explanation: User Account Control (UAC) ensures administrators and standard users run with filtered standard tokens by default, prompting for explicit elevation when an administrative task is required to prevent silent background system modifications.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a security baseline?
options: Guarantee that no vulnerability exists
Remove all deviations without regard to the system's role
Define a documented, approved configuration for assessing and maintaining security
Replace all change-control procedures
quiz.explanation: A security baseline (such as CIS Benchmarks or Microsoft Security Baselines) establishes an approved, documented configuration standard against which systems can be measured, audited, and protected from configuration drift.

quiz.question: What should an administrator do if an application fails after a hardening change?
options: Investigate the evidence, validate the configuration, and apply a controlled correction or rollback
Disable every security control permanently
Ignore the failure and close the change ticket
Grant the application unrestricted administrative privileges by default
quiz.explanation: Hardening requires disciplined change control. When an unexpected regression occurs, the administrator should inspect error logs, audit records, and permissions, and either tune the specific rule or enact a documented rollback.

theorySections.title: Operating System Security Fundamentals
paragraphs: The operating system's role as a resource mediator, the OS attack surface, layered defense, and distinguishing vulnerabilities from misconfigurations.

Operating system security is the practice of protecting the OS, its configuration, accounts, processes, files, system interfaces, and administrative functions against unauthorized access and misuse. The OS mediates access to CPU, memory, filesystem objects, network sockets, hardware peripherals, and security principals.
A flaw or bug in binary logic (e.g. heap buffer overflow or use-after-free). Requires vendor source patch or recompilation.
An administrative setting or policy choice (e.g. leaving SSH root login permitted, mode 777 on sensitive logs, disabled host firewall).

NIST SP 800-123 emphasizes: Hardening is not the act of disabling as many features as possible. It is the disciplined process of making the system's actual configuration match its documented security requirements.

theorySections.title: Windows Security, Permissions, and Privilege Management
paragraphs: Security Principals, SIDs, Access Tokens, NTFS Permissions, UAC token filtering, and Windows LAPS password rotation.
Windows relies on Security Identifiers (SIDs) and Access Tokens. NTFS permissions govern objects, supporting Full Control, Modify, Read & Execute, Read, and Write.
Splits administrative logins into a filtered standard token and an elevated token. Restricts silent execution of malware requiring admin rights.
